How to Outperform the 4% CPF SA Rate with S$30,000
article:
A guaranteed 4% return is a tough benchmark to beat, which is why Singapore’s CPF Special Account (CPF SA) remains a cornerstone of local financial planning.
Still, there are plenty of long-term investors who aim for better returns by investing in solid companies.
So here’s the question: Can S$30,000 in stocks turn into something that consistently tops that 4%?
Why the CPF Special Account Is Such a High Benchmark
The CPF remains Singapore’s financial bedrock, guaranteeing 2.5% on the Ordinary Account and 4% or more on Special, MediSave, and Retirement Accounts.
Your money compounds safely in the background, completely insulated from market turbulence, fees, or active management.
However, clearing that risk-free 4% hurdle in the open market is tricky once trading fees and volatility enter the frame.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) expects core inflation to average 1.5% to 2.5% in 2026, which leaves the CPF SA’s 4% delivering a real return of around 1.5% to 2.5%.
That is a respectable floor – but it is a floor, and savers chasing more than inflation-plus-a-bit turn to the
CPF Investment Scheme
(CPFIS) to give their long-term wealth extra horsepower.
Can Stocks Beat 4% Over the Long Term?
To beat the 4% hurdle, quality stocks rely on three engines: capital growth from rising earnings, steady dividends, and long-term compounding through reinvestment.
Major STI constituent banks like
DBS Group
(SGX: D05) often yield 4% to 6% in dividends alone.
However, CPF SA provides absolute certainty.
Equities offer higher expected returns, but investors must endure short-term price volatility to capture that equity risk premium over the long run.
What Could S$30,000 Look Like Over Time?
In early years, the gap between a 4% CPF SA rate and a 6% to 8% stock return seems modest.
But give it three decades, and the picture changes completely.
Here is how a single S$30,000 lump sum grows across different return rates:

After 30 years, an 8% return takes you past S$300,000, which is over three times what you’d get sticking with 4%.
That divide is the real reason people with patience ride out the ups and downs in the market.
What Kind of Investments Could Potentially Beat 4%?
Blue-Chip Stocks
These are
established, market-leading companies
that offer long-term capital stability alongside resilient cash dividends that frequently exceed 4%.
DBS
posted a 1Q2026 net profit of S$2.93 billion and declared a quarterly dividend of S$0.81 per share.
At a share price of S$74.02 as of 31 July 2026, that works out to an annualised yield of around 4.4% (inclusive of capital returns), topping the 4% CPF SA hurdle on payout yield alone.
Similarly,
Singapore Telecommunications Limited
(SGX: Z74) delivered an FY2026 underlying net profit of S$2.77 billion and reported a total annual dividend of S$0.185 per share.
At a share price of S$4.38, this works out to a yield of roughly 4.2%, clearing the Special Account’s 4% bar.
Singapore Real Estate Investment Trusts (S-REITs)
REITs like
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U), or CICT, pool income-generating properties to distribute regular rental payouts, making them ideal for income investors.
CICT reported a 1Q2026 net property income of S$314.4 million, up 7.9% YoY.
At a unit price of S$2.44, its distribution yield of around 4.4% outpaces the CPF SA through resilient commercial real estate cash flows.
Another popular S-REIT amongst local investors is
Mapletree Logistics Trust
(SGX: M44U), which generated an FY2025/2026 distribution per unit (DPU) of S$0.07262.
At S$1.22 per unit, the distribution yield works out to roughly 6%.
Broad Market & REIT ETFs
Funds like the SPDR Straits Times Index ETF (SGX: ES3) or the Lion-Phillip S-REIT ETF (SGX: CLR) offer
instant diversification
across top blue chips or property trusts, capturing steady market growth and income payouts well above 4% while mitigating individual stock risk.
The
SPDR STI ETF
, for example, offers a trailing yield of 3.1% with long-term capital appreciation.
The Risks of Chasing Higher Returns
Outperforming CPF requires accepting market volatility, since capital values fluctuate and dividends are never guaranteed.
Beyond market swings, the biggest threats are panic-selling during downturns and trying to time the market.
Achieving higher long-term returns demands accepting greater uncertainty and having the discipline to ride out temporary losses.
A Smarter Way to Think About CPF and Investing
It isn’t an either-or decision.
The smartest strategy leverages both systems for their distinct strengths.
Use the CPF SA as a rock-solid foundation for guaranteed capital preservation while relying on equities as a long-term engine to beat inflation and build passive income.
Pairing CPF’s risk-free floor with market upside secures your retirement baseline while giving your wealth genuine room to grow.
Who Should Consider Investing Instead of Keeping Everything in CPF?
If you already have a strong emergency fund and can handle the market’s ups and downs without losing sleep, then equity investing makes sense for you.
Don’t get caught up comparing CPF’s steady, guaranteed rates with overly hopeful stock market returns, and avoid jumping at eye-catching dividend yields.
A high payout means nothing if your investment loses value or the dividends dry up.
Instead, focus on total returns and make sure you’re investing in solid businesses.
Get Smart: Aim to Beat CPF Only If You Understand the Price
That 4% guaranteed interest rate from your CPF Special Account is solid.
Yes, good stocks, REITs, or ETFs may offer better yields, but you have to be prepared to stomach market volatility.
Use your CPF as a safety net and let your investments handle the heavy lifting for long-term growth.
That way, you get stability and a shot at building real long-term wealth.
If you’re planning to put S$100,000 into dividend stocks, the highest yield on the list isn’t always the safest one. Some of those numbers come from companies stretching to keep the payout going, right before they cut it. title: AI chip designer DeepX’s value surges to US$2.2 bil in funding
article:
(Aug 3): South Korean AI chip designer DeepX Co has secured fresh funding at roughly four times its previous valuation, in a sign of sustained enthusiasm for companies involved in the artificial intelligence boom.

The Pangyo-based startup was valued at about 3.14 trillion won in its latest deal, according to people with knowledge of the matter. DeepX has signed the first tranche of its Series D round, securing 42 billion won from existing backers BNW Investment Co and DS Asset Management Co, said the people, asking not to be named discussing private information.

The company, a developer of semiconductor architecture tailored for AI tasks, is in talks for additional funding of up to 300 billion won. It's seeking to raise it by September, the people said. The company is seeking a post-money valuation of as much as 3.5 trillion won when the round is completed, they said.

DeepX’s semiconductors are intended for AI work and applications outside of data centres, where power and cost efficiency are highly prized. It has targeted robotics and smarter electronics as key areas for deployment. Its surging valuation shows confidence in the company’s ability to ramp up its commercial deals. In April, DeepX said it secured more than 30 mass-production contracts from customers across eight countries.

title: China Mobile said to be to mulling stake sale in Thailand’s True — Bloomberg
article:
(Aug 3): China Mobile Ltd is considering selling its minority stake in Thailand’s telecommunications company True Corp, according to people familiar with the situation.

The Chinese mobile and internet firm is working with an adviser to sound out initial interest from prospective buyers in its stake in True, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing a private matter.

True shares fell as much as 4.9% in Bangkok, the biggest intraday drop in more than a month, before paring some losses. The stock has gained 28% this year, giving the company a market value of about US$14.5 billion. At that level, China Mobile’s holding would be worth about US$1.1 billion.

China Mobile has roughly a 7.8% stake in True, according to the Thai group’s latest annual report.

Deliberations are ongoing and may not lead to a transaction, the people said. A representative for China Mobile didn’t immediately respond to requests seeking comment.

Naureen Quayum, head of investor relations at True, said China Mobile has told the company it intends to be a long-term shareholder of the Thai carrier and has no intention of exiting its position.

See also: Is Labubu China’s answer to Mickey Mouse?

True merged with the Thai unit of Norway’s Telenor ASA in 2023. Earlier this year, Telenor agreed to sell its stake in True to Arise Digital Technology Co for a total value of US$3.9 billion.

True has more than 48 million mobile subscribers and also operates home broadband and cable television.

China Mobile is the world’s largest wireless carrier by subscribers and the country’s primary provider of mobile, internet, and digital infrastructure services. The state-owned telecommunications giant has about one billion mobile subscribers and hundreds of millions of broadband users.

title: Chinese tea chains are brewing a new US obsession
article:
NEW YORK (Aug 3): Brooklyn resident Steven Sparling didn’t expect a cup of tea to be worth standing in line for two hours. But a new Heytea location on New York’s Upper East Side convinced him.

“Once we got in, I realised why there was that big wait,” the 51-year-old public-school teacher said while sipping on guava green tea on a recent summer afternoon. “I’m not so much into tea, but I’m getting more into it now.”

A wave of Chinese tea chains including Heytea, Teapulse and Mixue are winning converts from coffee as they rapidly expand in New York and beyond. They’re building on the bubble tea craze of recent years while capitalising on strong demand for new beverages and flavour profiles — as well as a growing interest in everything Chinese.

Customers are enamoured with hard-to-get ingredients such as the perfume lemons, imported from China and found at Heytea, and osmanthus tea at Teapulse. The brightly coloured beverages that look fantastic on Instagram and TikTok are also part of the draw.

Alexa Lantin, who was visiting Heytea with her husband and baby, said she’s looking for new flavours, noting that everyone seems to love ube at the moment. “People want that unique flavour,” the 31-year-old said of the vibrant purple yam that tastes like a milder sweet potato.

Her husband, Adrian Apolonio, said he preferred the atmosphere over big coffee houses, where he sees “more people using it as a workspace”. At Heytea, “there’s a lot of people who come here with friends, so they’re usually chatting and sitting down for a while”.

See also: Danone sales climb on high protein, medical nutrition demand

In addition to tea drinks fused with fruit, all of the chains offer milk-based options, and many sell cheese teas — served cold with a cheese-based foam topping. Mixue specialises in teas paired with soft-serve ice cream in flavours such as brown sugar pearl sundae and classic cone.

Heytea’s beverages range from US$4 ($5.13) for the original cloud jasmine tea to a cloud matcha latte that tops out at about US$8, while Mixue’s run from US$2 for lemonade to the US$5 mango pomelo taro fruit tea.

Tea’s perceived health benefits also draw customers. Alejandro Rios, Sparling’s partner, says Heytea’s drinks are healthier than those served at larger US-based chains, listing seed oils in mixed beverages in particular as something he’s looking to avoid. “That’s something you don’t need. And here’s something that’s clean,” he said while celebrating his 50th birthday with his laptop open and a classic matcha latte in hand.

See also: Why Guinness keeps growing while beer sales worldwide fizz out

While tea without additives is deemed healthy, many of the beverages offered at the tea chains wouldn't fall under that category due to high levels of sugar and calories.

Growth is coming fast. Teapulse is approaching 10 New York stores and is looking to expand into 25 states, while Heytea has more than 40 locations in New York, California and other states. Mixue Group, which has nearly 50,000 locations worldwide and went public last year, now has six stores in New York and a similar number in California. Mollytea, which was founded in Shenzen, China, is also in the US, although a legal dispute with local operators has clouded the outlook.

Teapulse co-founder Alvin Zhang said there’s a broader shift in habits as more consumers turn to tea for caffeine over coffee. Some are establishing an afternoon tea routine — a traditionally weak part of the day that restaurant companies have long battled to overcome. He adds that smaller companies like Teapulse can move faster than bigger chains to respond to feedback and capitalise on emerging trends, such as blending different tea varieties with ingredients like boba and cheese foam.

While many restaurants are struggling with lower consumer spending and rising costs for labour and ingredients, the beverage category is a bright spot. David Portalin, senior vice-president at Circana, a market research company, says drinks remain a “permissible indulgence” for consumers who are otherwise cutting back on spending.

Huy Do, a market researcher at Datassential, says consumers “see sub-US$10 purchases as ways to pick them up and make them feel better about their everyday routines”. This is attributed to “little treat” culture where consumers bypass substantial purchases but are willing to splurge on low-stake indulgences. He adds that consumers appear less sensitive to beverage prices than meal prices, in part because the purchases are often impulsive.

“There’s a lot of really interesting psychological justification that happens,” he said.

title: South Korea unveils higher taxes on pricey, investment homes
article:
(Aug 3): South Korea proposed a property tax overhaul that would increase levies on high-value homes and investment properties as President Lee Jae Myung’s administration seeks to curb speculation in a housing market that has posted relentless gains.

The measures would raise holding taxes on expensive homes while preserving or expanding breaks for owner-occupiers, with the government casting the changes as a way to improve fairness by shifting more of the burden to expensive properties. Tax benefits would also increasingly depend on how long owners actually live in a property, rather than how long they have owned it.

“Under the principle that a home is a place for living, not an asset for buying, we will rationally reform the real estate tax system so that a housing market centered on actual residence can take root,” Finance Minister Koo Yun Cheol said in a briefing.

Most owner-occupied homes valued at up to about three billion won would continue to receive preferential tax treatment under the proposal. Homes above that threshold would gradually face higher holding taxes under what the government described as a normalisation of the property tax system. The package would also tighten taxes on multiple-home owners and non-resident homeowners.

The tax overhaul marks the latest attempt by Lee’s administration to rein in a housing market that has defied months of restrictive policies. Despite stricter mortgage rules, warnings against speculation and pledges to accelerate home construction, prices have continued to climb, leaving the government searching for new ways to cool demand without inflicting broader economic damage.

That has prompted the government to tackle the issue by tax revision. It plans to phase in higher comprehensive real estate taxes through 2028, while temporarily easing capital-gains tax surcharges for owners of multiple homes to encourage them to sell properties before the tougher tax regime takes full effect.

See also: Southeast Asia’s factory activity bounces back from 11-month low

The tax package is part of a broader housing tightening measure. Properties in designated speculative areas are already subject to stricter mortgage rules and land transaction permit requirements. The tax changes add another layer by increasing the cost of holding high-value and investment properties.

The overhaul comes as Seoul apartment prices extended their weekly gains to about 18 months, underscoring the housing market’s resilience despite a series of government measures, including expansion of speculative zones around Seoul and major semiconductor hubs. Persistently rising home prices have also added to financial stability risks watched closely by the central bank.

The tax revision package is due to be submitted to the National Assembly before Sept 3.

title: AI skills more valuable than MBAs, 86% of finance executives say
article:
(Aug 3): Executives are questioning the value of an MBA in the AI era.

Some 86% of the more than 1,000 US financial services executives surveyed by consulting firm PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP say they think AI training is more valuable than an MBA for many new hires, reflecting the urgency companies face in adopting the technology effectively.

The survey, released Monday, showed companies are willing to pay accordingly: 91% of executives said they’re increasing compensation for employees with AI skills.

“There is a clear need for people that understand not just what an agent is but how do you build them? How do you think about managing them?” said Peter Pollini, who leads PwC’s financial services industry practice. He added that many firms are looking for workers with technical skills to help them implement the AI use cases they have identified.

Whether an MBA is worth the investment has long been the subject of debate, particularly as the typical total cost of the degree nears US$300,000. As tuitions rise, prospective students are increasingly scrutinising what they’ll get in return.

Universities, meanwhile, have spotted an opportunity. Prestigious business schools at Harvard University, the University of Pennsylvania and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology are offering a growing list of AI-themed executive education courses that are shorter and cheaper than a degree programme and offer certificates. At MIT, for example, students can take a five-day course called “Leading the AI-Driven Organization” for about US$13,000.

See also: Alibaba releases AI model with performance rivalling Anthropic

Growing demand for AI-savvy workers has led some companies, including software makers International Business Machines Corp, Shopify Inc and Cloudflare Inc, to ramp up entry-level hiring, betting that recent Gen Z graduates will be able to do more with AI tools than existing employees.

title: Iran says Hormuz talks underway after Trump calls off strikes
article:
(Aug 3): Iran suggested negotiations to get more ships moving through the Strait of Hormuz are making progress, after US President Donald Trump called off what he said was a major attack on the Islamic Republic.

Oil fell on Monday, with Brent crude down about 4.5% to just over US$83 a barrel, after Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said discussions between Tehran and Oman over management of the strait are in the final stages.

Trump said Sunday that a deal to open the waterway may be close and that new unspecified talks with Iran would begin on Monday.

Still, there’s little clarity on the Iran-Oman negotiations and no sign the Islamic Republic is willing to allow vessels free passage through the waterway, which Trump has demanded. Instead, Iran said it’s talking to Oman about a new route and not about whether the strait as a whole will be open or closed.

The discussions with Oman are about a “temporary” route to ensure the safety of ships, Esmail Baghaei, an Iranian foreign ministry spokesman, said on Monday. “We are not currently negotiating with the United States.”

Last week, Bloomberg reported that Muscat and Tehran were discussing reopening the so-called middle passage through Hormuz. It has, however, been mined by Iran, according to people familiar with the matter, and could have to be cleared before vessels use it on a regular basis.

See also: Euro-area inflation strengthens as US-Iran strikes boost oil

The chokepoint, a vital conduit for supplies of oil, liquefied natural gas and other commodities such as fertilisers, remains all but shut. Hardly any ships are sailing through, at least with their transponders turned on. Most that do are going on a northern route close to Iran’s shores with Iranian permission, or on a southern one nearby Omani territory.

Trump, early on Sunday Iran time, said he had cancelled strikes — the likes of which he claimed have “not seen since World War II” — after lobbying from Iran and Middle Eastern countries. He later said Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar had all urged him to give diplomacy more time.

Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman held a call with Trump over the weekend. The kingdom’s de facto leader “stressed the need to prioritise dialogue to reduce escalation and the importance of making every possible effort to achieve calm”, according to the main Saudi news agency.

Gulf Arab states are allies of the US but have become exasperated by the continuation of the war, now in its sixth month. They are concerned that any escalation would see Iran lash out by firing more drones and missiles at them, damaging their infrastructure and hurting their economies.

Iran has regularly attacked the likes of Kuwait and Bahrain in the past two months, during skirmishes with the US. Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar have suffered less, but have seen their ships hit near Hormuz. Saudi Arabia has also been attacked by Iran-backed militias in Iraq and by the Houthis, based in Yemen, in the past two weeks.

Trump signalled he wouldn’t wait long for a diplomatic resolution and urged mediators and Iran to “rapidly make a deal”. It must include, he said, the “immediate, complete, and total opening” of the strait, as well as “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat”.

The US, he said, remains “locked and loaded”. He suggested the weekend strikes would have been carried out with Israel, which isn’t known to have struck Iran since a first ceasefire deal in April.

While implying the attacks would have been the biggest since the Iran war erupted in late February, Trump said he is “not looking to kill people”. US embassies across the region on Saturday had warned Americans to be prepared for flight cancellations and airspace closures.

The president previously said he would step up the intensity of bombing until Iran reopened the strait. He threatened to eventually hit the country’s civilian infrastructure and power plants, something Tehran has warned it would retaliate against fiercely.

Israel, which launched the war alongside the US but wasn’t party to an initial Washington-Iran peace deal in June, is waiting out the latest diplomatic push, according to a member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s security cabinet, Zev Elkin.

There’s “some kind of vector toward an agreement between Iran and Oman”, he told local Army Radio on Sunday.

title: Nissan keeps outlook as latest quarter shows turnaround progress
article:
(Aug 3): Nissan Motor Co’s quarterly profit rose as the carmaker looks to build on progress from the early stages of its restructuring plan.

The Japanese carmaker reported ¥78 billion in operating profit during the three-month period between August and June, the company said Monday, exceeding analysts’ estimates for ¥6 billion and marking a big improvement from the ¥79 billion loss a year earlier. Net sales were ¥3 trillion, in line with projections.

Nissan kept its ¥200 billion profit and ¥13 trillion revenue outlook for the fiscal year ending March 2027. The carmaker revised its sales volume outlook to 3.15 million units from 3.3 million, citing a more challenging business environment, particularly in China.

The results offer an early indication of CEO Ivan Espinosa’s bid to stabilise Nissan after years of sliding sales and management turmoil. His turnaround hinges on aggressive cost cuts, a faster vehicle-development cycle and stronger performance in the US and China, even as the carmaker contends with currency swings, rising input costs and intensifying competition from Chinese rivals.

Still, outdated products, revolving-door leadership and a failed tie-up with Honda Motor Co have left the Japanese carmaker struggling to fend for itself in the global automobile industry’s rapid shift toward software-focused, battery-powered cars.

title: MUFG beats estimates to seal strong quarter for Japan banks
article:
(Aug 3): Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group Inc’s profit rose more than analysts anticipated, capping another bumper quarter for Japan’s biggest banks.

Net income climbed 48% from a year earlier to ¥809.4 billion in the three months ended June 30, Japan’s largest lender said Monday. That exceeded analysts’ ¥633.4 billion average estimate and put the firm on course for another record year. All its business units performed, led by global markets and corporate and investment banking business.

Lending income jumped, as MUFG joined its peers in benefiting from rising domestic interest rates and robust loan demand. The firm also got a boost from its position as the largest shareholder in Morgan Stanley, whose profit jumped thanks to a boom in equity trading and wealth management.

MUFG kept its forecast for net income to reach an all-time high of ¥2.7 trillion in the year ending March 31. Last week, Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group Inc and Mizuho Financial Group Inc also reported results that exceeded analysts’ expectations. Mizuho, the third-largest lender, raised its annual profit forecast and expanded a share buyback programme.

A weaker yen has also been pushing up the value of the banks’ earnings generated abroad, although the currency has gained in recent days as US and Japanese authorities coordinated their first joint intervention in 15 years.

See also: BOJ holds rate steady at 1%, upgrades view on economy

See also: Toyota sales fall for fifth month on Middle East turmoil, China slump

Return on equity, a gauge of how well the company uses investors’ capital, climbed to 14.4% from 10.8% a year earlier, MUFG said in a presentation.

The results were also lifted by income from offloading shares held in client companies, at a time when Japanese stocks touched a record. Its gains on sales of equity securities more than tripled from a year earlier to ¥98.9 billion.

Rising interest rates and geopolitical risks have yet to make a sizeable dent in credit quality. Bad-loan costs totalled ¥72 billion in the quarter, well within the Tokyo-based bank’s full-year projection of ¥350 billion.

Shares of MUFG closed 0.1% lower in Tokyo before the results, slightly paring this year’s gain to 43%. Japanese bank shares have surged since the Bank of Japan ended its negative interest-rate policy in March 2024, letting them charge more for loans.

Led by CEO Junichi Hanzawa, MUFG has revived a goal of becoming one of the world’s most valuable banks. The lender last month briefly overtook Toyota Motor Corp as the biggest Japanese company by market capitalisation.

Morgan Stanley accounted for more than a quarter of MUFG’s net income in the period. The Japanese bank took a stake in the Wall Street firm at the height of the global financial crisis in 2008, and the companies jointly operate a pair of securities ventures in Tokyo.

title: AstraZeneca is said to have explored Bristol Myers merger — Bloomberg
article:
(Aug 3): AstraZeneca Plc has explored an acquisition of Bristol Myers Squibb Co, a megadeal that would create one of the world’s largest drugmakers, according to people familiar with the matter.

The companies have held early-stage discussions about combining, the people added, asking not to be identified because the matter is private. Astra shares plunged on the news in early London trading, declining as much as 7.8%.

It’s unclear if discussions are ongoing or whether they will result in a transaction, the people cautioned.

A representative for AstraZeneca declined to comment and Bristol Myers Squibb couldn’t immediately be reached for comment on the talks, which were first reported by the Financial Times.

Bristol Myers Squibb, which has a US$133.4 billion market capitalisation, could provide AstraZeneca with a bigger foothold in the US market. AstraZeneca has a market value of about £195.9 billion.

Bristol is preparing for the loss of patent protection for some of its biggest products, including the blood thinner Eliquis and cancer drug Opdivo. Together, they make up about half of Bristol’s sales.

See also: Maybank buys remaining stake in Etiqa’s holding company from Ageas for RM4.83 bil

Last week, Bristol reported quarterly sales of US$13 billion, its highest ever. The growth was primarily driven by newer products like the blood cancer treatment Breyanzi, Opdualag for skin cancer and the heart drug Camzyos.

Under chief executive officer Pascal Soriot, AstraZeneca has become a cancer drug powerhouse with a string of blockbuster medicines. Soon after he took over as CEO in 2012, Soriot fended off a takeover attempt from Pfizer Inc that triggered UK government involvement over fears of losing a key British company.

See also: A-Sonic Aerospace to acquire 60% of JGL Group for $15.216 mil

AstraZeneca is currently the second-largest company on the London Stock Exchange. It’s increasingly been pivoting to the US, and last year upgraded its US stock listing to the New York Stock Exchange, replacing its American Depositary Receipts on Nasdaq, while keeping its headquarters and primary listing in London.

The drugmaker is on track for an ambitious target of US$80 billion in sales by 2030, and it’s hoping to break into the lucrative weight-loss market with multiple drugs in development.

Soriot has previously told Bloomberg that when he gets pitches on diseases outside the company’s core areas, “I always say no, because the risk of making the wrong bet increases rapidly if you go out of your area of expertise.”

An analyst at Mizuho argued investors are likely to push back on the idea of a merger, since AstraZeneca is expected to grow earnings per share at 10% or more over the next five years and Bristol Myers’ earnings per share may shrink through the rest of the decade.

“Investors will argue that AstraZeneca does not need Bristol Myers, only the other way around and unless there are massive deal synergies that offset revenue/earnings declines this merger is tough to justify,” Jared Holz, Mizuho’s healthcare specialist, wrote in a note on Sunday.

However, Holz said his initial thought was, “If there was ever a time for a deal like this, it would arguably be now,” citing the Trump administration’s fairly lenient stance on merger activity.

Meanwhile, antitrust concerns were a key part of a note from BMO Capital Markets analyst Evan Seigerman.

“With both Bristol and Astra reaching market caps well over US$100 billion, we see a direct buyout of either company as unlikely,” he said, adding that significant overlaps in areas like non-small cell lung cancer also “lower the chance of a merger materialising, in our view.”

If a deal is completed, it would rank as the largest pharmaceutical deal of all time, according to data compiled by Bloomberg News, topping Bristol’s US$74 billion takeover of Celgene in 2019.

title: Maybank buys remaining stake in Etiqa’s holding company from Ageas for RM4.83 bil
article:
KUALA LUMPUR (Aug 3): Malayan Banking Bhd (KL:MAYBANK) is acquiring the remaining 30.95% stake in Etiqa's holding company, Maybank Ageas Holdings Bhd, from Belgian insurer Ageas SA for RM4.83 billion, giving Malaysia's largest lender full ownership of its insurance and takaful business.

In a statement on Monday, Maybank said it had signed an implementation agreement with Ageas Insurance International NV to acquire the remaining stake in its 69.05%-owned subsidiary, Maybank Ageas.

Maybank Ageas is the holding company for Etiqa's operations in Malaysia and Singapore, offering life and general insurance as well as...(click on link for full story theedgemalaysia.com)

title: Shein to weigh cost reset for late backers before Hong Kong IPO — Bloomberg
article:
(Aug 3): Shein Global Holdings Ltd is considering lowering the cost of investment for late backers that came in at an up to US$64 billion ($82 billion) valuation, people familiar with the matter said, as the fast-fashion retailer prepares for a Hong Kong listing at a much lower value.

The company may hand out a combination of cash payouts and free additional Class B shares to investors in its Series pre-D, Series D and Series D+ rounds, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing a private matter. The move will help lower the cost base from those investors to a roughly US$40 billion valuation, which will be more aligned with the planned initial public offering, the people said.

Considerations are ongoing and no final decisions have been made, the people said. The amount of the cash payouts and additional shares handed to these investors will depend on the valuation Shein gets in the IPO, they added.

Coatue Management, HSG and General Atlantic are among the investors that participated in Shein’s Series Pre-D, D and D+ funding rounds, according to the company’s prospectus, which also mentioned plans to compensate some investors via cash and Class B shares to match the IPO, without disclosing any terms.

Founded in mainland China and now headquartered in Singapore, Shein operates as an online fast-fashion retailer known for its direct-from-supplier model. The company, which serves consumers across 160 markets, has secured a key approval from the China Securities Regulatory Commission.

The company disclosed slowing profitability and revenue growth in the first detailed look at its finances ahead of the listing. It posted a loss of US$99 million in the first three months of 2026, versus a US$395 million profit a year earlier, while revenue rose just 1.1% to US$9.05 billion.
